judged_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8-10 — `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` call `.toString()` on ZodString/ZodOptional *instances* (not string values), both yielding the literal key `"[object Object]"` (the second overwrites the first), so `minimumTokenResponseSchema` actually reduces to `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }` — it does not implement "any property with a number is the expiry" or "allow other properties" as the comments claim; there is no such dynamic/by-value-type key matching capability in zod, so when credential-sync is enabled the schema silently validates only that `access_token` is a string and enforces nothing about expiry, making the "minimum token response" contract vacuous. Confidence 100, Severity P1.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. These expressions evaluate immediately to a fixed string (the `toString()` of a Zod type instance), not a dynamic “any key” matcher, so the object schema ends up with one or two literal property names rather than validating arbitrary keys. Zod doesn’t support “any property whose value is a number” via computed keys like this, and the second computed key can also collide/overwrite depending on the string result. As a result, when credential sync is enabled, the ‘minimum’ schema effectively only guarantees `access_token` (and not an expiry) and does not actually allow/validate arbitrary properties as the comments claim.
